d.title: Every string method returns a NEW string
d.caption: A `str` is immutable, so there is no method that edits one in place — `s.upper()` hands back a new object and leaves `s` alone. Half the string questions in an interview are really testing whether you know that.
cells: a list, then a string back

d.title: List operations, by cost
d.caption: The cost column is what the follow-up question is usually about. `insert(0, x)` and `pop(0)` shift every element, which is why a queue built on a list degrades and a `deque` does not.
cells: room is over-allocated at the end
a scan — use a set for membership

d.title: Four containers, four answers
d.caption: Most of this set is one table. The `hashable` column is the one that decides what can be a dict key or go inside a set — and it is why a `list` cannot, but a `tuple` of immutables can.

d.title: What a dict lookup actually does
d.caption: Knowing these four steps answers most dictionary questions at once: why keys must be hashable, why a mutated key is lost, why lookup is O(1) on average, and why two unequal objects with the same hash still work.

items.label: hash(key)
items.desc: an int — which is why an unhashable key raises TypeError

items.label: pick a slot from the hash
items.desc: the low bits index the table, so it is a direct jump rather than a scan

items.label: compare with ==
items.desc: a hash collision is normal; equality decides, so __hash__ and __eq__ must agree

items.label: probe the next slot on a clash
items.desc: which is why a dict degrades to O(n) only in the pathological case

d.title: break, continue and the else nobody expects
d.caption: `for … else` runs the else clause only when the loop finished **without** a break, which makes it a search idiom rather than a curiosity. That is the question in this set people get wrong.

d.title: LEGB: where a name is looked up
d.caption: Read top down. A bare assignment creates a **local** name, which is why reading a global then assigning to it raises `UnboundLocalError` — the commonest scope question there is.

items.label: Enclosing
items.sub: a surrounding function’s locals — what a closure captures

items.label: Built-in
items.sub: len, print, range — shadowed by any name above

d.title: map, filter, reduce — and why a comprehension usually wins
d.caption: All three are lazy in Python 3 except `reduce`, which consumes. The interview answer worth having is that a comprehension is clearer for map and filter, and `reduce` is the one with no comprehension equivalent.

nodes.label: map(f, …)
nodes.sub: lazy — one value at a time

d.title: The iterator protocol is two methods
d.caption: A generator is just a convenient way to get an object with these two methods. Once that clicks, the questions about laziness, one-shot consumption and memory all have the same answer.

items.label: iter(obj) → an iterator
items.desc: __iter__; a for loop calls this once, at the start

items.label: next(it) → the next value
items.desc: __next__; the function body resumes where it yielded

items.label: StopIteration
items.desc: raised when exhausted, and the for loop swallows it

items.label: and it is now spent
items.desc: an iterator is one-shot — a second loop over it yields nothing

d.title: try, except, else, finally — in execution order
d.caption: The `else` clause runs only when the `try` body raised nothing, and `finally` runs whatever happens — including on a `return`. A `return` inside `finally` discards the exception, which is the trap this set is built around.

items.label: try
items.desc: the guarded body

items.label: except
items.desc: only if it raised, and only the first matching clause

items.label: else
items.desc: only if it did NOT raise — so put the follow-on work here, not in try

items.label: finally
items.desc: always — and a return here swallows the exception

d.title: What `with` guarantees
d.caption: `__exit__` runs on the way out whatever happens — normal end, `return`, or exception. Returning a truthy value from it **suppresses** the exception, which is the question people miss.

items.label: __enter__()
items.desc: its return value is what as binds

items.label: the body
items.desc: may return, break or raise

items.label: __exit__(exc_type, exc, tb)
items.desc: always called — this is the guarantee you are buying

items.label: return True to suppress
items.desc: falsy (or None) re-raises; truthy swallows the exception

d.title: How an import is resolved
d.caption: Six questions, and they all come back to this order. The first entry of `sys.path` is the script's own directory, which is why a local `random.py` shadows the standard library — the classic import bug.

items.label: sys.modules
items.desc: already imported? return it — so a module body runs ONCE

items.label: sys.path, in order
items.desc: the script’s directory first, then PYTHONPATH, then site-packages

items.label: execute the module body
items.desc: top to bottom, once; this is where a circular import bites

items.label: bind the name locally
items.desc: import x.y binds x; from x import y binds y

d.title: The four regex calls that get confused
d.caption: `match` anchors at the start, `search` does not, and `fullmatch` requires the whole string. Most “why does my pattern not match” question is one of these three being the wrong call.
cells: a list of strings or tuples

d.title: collections, by the problem each one solves
d.caption: Thirty-five questions over six types. The right answer to most of them is naming the problem the type removes — usually a `KeyError`, a manual counter, or an O(n) pop from the front.

cells.text: the KeyError on first touch — a factory supplies the default
O(n) pop(0) — both ends are O(1)
indexing a tuple by position and forgetting what [2] was
little now that dict keeps order — but move_to_end and == still differ

d.title: Three kinds of concurrency, one decision
d.caption: The GIL column decides everything. Threads do not run Python bytecode in parallel, so they help only when the work is waiting — and the right answer to “make this faster” depends entirely on whether the work is I/O or CPU.

d.title: How an object is freed
d.caption: Reference counting does almost all the work and cannot free a cycle, which is the whole reason a garbage collector exists alongside it. That one sentence answers most of this set.

items.label: refcount reaches zero
items.desc: freed immediately and deterministically — no collector involved

items.label: a cycle keeps it above zero
items.desc: a → b → a: unreachable, but each still holds a reference

items.label: the generational GC sweeps
items.desc: three generations; young objects are checked most often

items.label: __del__ can resurrect it
items.desc: which is why __del__ is not a destructor you should rely on

d.title: The gotchas these outputs are testing
d.caption: Forty-nine predict-the-output questions, and nearly all of them are one of these five. Recognising which one is being asked is most of the work.
rows: a is b vs a == b

cells.text: the default is made ONCE, at definition, and persists between calls
late binding — every lambda sees the final i, not the i at creation
identity against equality; small ints and short strings are interned
one list, two names — assignment never copies
False — binary floats cannot hold a tenth exactly

d.title: Creational patterns, by what they decide
d.caption: Each one moves a different decision out of the caller. Naming that decision is a better interview answer than reciting the structure — and in Python several collapse into a function or a module.
cells: a whole family of related classes
how a complex object is assembled
how to copy an existing instance

d.title: Structural patterns, by the mismatch each one hides
d.caption: All five sit between two things that do not quite fit. The interview distinction worth having is Adapter against Facade: one changes an interface, the other simplifies a subsystem.
cells: an interface you have and one you need

cells.text: wraps ONE object, changes its shape

a caller and an object, adding behaviour

d.title: Behavioural patterns, by what varies
d.caption: Each isolates one thing that changes. Strategy against State is the usual follow-up: Strategy is chosen from outside, State transitions itself from within.

cells.text: so it can be queued or undone

cells: the steps inside a fixed skeleton

d.title: The architectural shape most questions assume
d.caption: Dependencies point **inward**: the domain knows nothing about the database or the web layer. That single rule is what makes the layers testable, and it is what an interviewer is checking you can state.

items.label: the web layer
items.sub: HTTP, serialisation, status codes — no business rules

items.label: the domain
items.sub: entities and rules — knows nothing below it

items.label: infrastructure
items.sub: the database, queues, third parties — behind interfaces

d.title: What each version added
d.caption: Interviewers ask this to find out whether you have kept up. The two that change how you *write* code are the **walrus operator** (3.8) and **structural pattern matching** (3.10); the rest mostly change what you can express in a type — built-in generics in 3.9, `X | Y` unions in 3.10, the `type` alias syntax in 3.12. 3.11 added `ExceptionGroup` and `tomllib`, and 3.13 added free-threading as a build option.

d.title: The test pyramid, and where the questions land
d.caption: The shape is the argument: many fast tests at the bottom, few slow ones at the top. Most interview answers go wrong by putting integration work in a unit test — usually a real database call.

items.label: end-to-end
items.sub: a few — slow, flaky, highest confidence

items.label: integration
items.sub: real database, real HTTP, one boundary at a time

items.label: unit
items.sub: no I/O at all — thousands of them, in milliseconds

d.title: Reshaping: which call for which shape change
d.caption: Forty-nine questions, and the reshaping ones are where people stall. The distinction to hold is long against wide: `melt` goes long, `pivot` goes wide, and `pivot_table` is `pivot` that can aggregate.

d.title: A task queue, end to end
d.caption: Fifteen questions about this one picture. The two that matter: a task must be **idempotent**, because a broker guarantees at-least-once delivery, and a result nobody reads still costs you storage.

nodes.label: broker
nodes.sub: Redis or RabbitMQ — at least once

d.title: What Pydantic does to your input, in order
d.caption: Validation is **coercion first**, which is the thing people get wrong: `“5”` becomes `5` for an `int` field in v1 and in v2's lax mode, so a validator sees the converted value, not what arrived.

items.label: parse the raw input
items.desc: JSON or a dict — unknown keys ignored, or rejected if you say so

items.label: coerce each field to its type
items.desc: “5” → 5 in lax mode; strict mode refuses instead

items.label: run field validators
items.desc: they see the COERCED value, so validate the meaning, not the type

items.label: run model validators
items.desc: last — the only place a rule across two fields can live

d.title: Isolation levels, by what each one still allows
d.caption: The honest answer names the anomaly each level leaves behind. Postgres's default is Read Committed, so a repeated read inside one transaction can see different rows — which is where the lost-update bug lives.

d.title: A webhook you can trust
d.caption: The sender retries, so you will receive duplicates — that is normal, not a bug. These four steps are what the fifteen questions in this set are checking you would build.

items.label: verify the signature first
items.desc: before parsing anything; an unsigned webhook is anonymous input

items.label: return 2xx immediately
items.desc: acknowledge, then do the work — a slow handler looks like a failure

items.label: deduplicate on the event id
items.desc: delivery is at-least-once, so store the id and ignore repeats

items.label: process asynchronously
items.desc: a queue (i7.2), so a retry storm cannot take the endpoint down

d.title: Three ways to carry identity
d.caption: The revocation column is the one interviewers press on. A JWT cannot be un-issued, so a logout that must take effect immediately needs server state — which is most of the argument against stateless tokens.

d.caption: A map before the marathon. The left column is where they cluster, and the right is the thing each cluster is really testing — which is usually one mechanism rather than a fact.

d.title: What the second ninety cover
d.caption: The weight shifts from language to system. These questions have a follow-up about failure almost every time, so the answer worth rehearsing is what breaks rather than what the feature does.

cells.text: whether the work waits or computes — the GIL decides the answer
refcounting, and the cycle it cannot free
reaching for the batteries instead of hand-rolling
what you would mock, and what that stops the test proving
measuring before optimising, and knowing the cost table

d.title: What a senior interview is actually probing
d.caption: Eleven questions, and none of them are about syntax. The move from mid to senior is answering with a **trade-off and its cost** rather than a definition — and saying what you would measure.

items.label: trade-offs, not definitions
items.sub: name the cost of the thing you recommend

items.label: failure first
items.sub: what breaks, how you would see it, what you would do

items.label: measurement
items.sub: the number you would check before and after

items.label: scope and blast radius
items.sub: who is affected, and how you would limit it

items.label: the decision record
items.sub: why, written down, so the next person inherits the reasoning
